title: Why most AI integrations fail — and it is not the model
excerpt: When an AI integration underperforms, the instinct is to blame the model. In most cases the problem is upstream.
body:
When an AI integration underperforms in production, the instinct is to blame the model. Switch providers, upgrade to the latest version, try a different prompting strategy. In most of the failure cases I have worked through, the problem was not the model. It was the architecture around it.

The three architectural failure patterns

Weak data contracts. The model is only as good as the data it receives. In many integrations, the data pipeline was designed for an earlier version of the system and delivers information at the wrong granularity, with inconsistent formatting, or without the context the model needs to produce useful output. Fixing this requires treating data quality as a first-class concern upstream of the model — not as something the model will "figure out."

No evaluation framework. Teams that ship AI integrations without a way to measure quality have no way to know whether they are improving or degrading. Over time, prompt changes, model updates, and data drift accumulate. Without evaluation infrastructure, you discover the degradation from user complaints rather than from monitoring.

Integration patterns designed for determinism. Many AI integrations are bolted onto systems that were designed for deterministic, synchronous APIs. The mismatch between that architecture and the probabilistic, latency-variable nature of LLM calls creates brittleness that shows up under real-world conditions. Designing AI integration points natively — with appropriate timeouts, retry strategies, fallback logic, and output validation — dramatically improves reliability.
